articles.title: How shorter antibiotic courses are changing inpatient conversations
articles.dek: An illustrative overview of the evidence questions hospitalists should ask before shortening treatment.
summary: For selected infections, researchers have investigated whether a shorter antibiotic course can work as well as a longer one. The right duration depends on the infection, clinical stability, source control and patient-specific risks.

For hospitalists, the practical question is not simply how many days to prescribe. It is whether the diagnosis is secure, whether the patient is improving, and whether a specific guideline or trial actually applies to that patient.
This is a teaching example, not a report of a new study. Before changing treatment, check the current guideline and original research for the specific syndrome.
articles.why: Potential implications for stewardship, adverse effects and discharge planning.
articles.evidence: Educational illustration; no specific study cited.

articles.title: Rethinking discharge readiness beyond vital signs
articles.dek: Why functional status, support systems and follow-up matter alongside medical stability.
summary: Discharge readiness is broader than normal vital signs. Mobility, cognition, medication access and caregiver capacity can affect whether a patient can safely manage after leaving the hospital.

A structured handoff can document unresolved risks and who is responsible for follow-up. This is particularly important when therapy assessments and family concerns differ from the medical team's assessment.
articles.why: A useful framework for safer transitions of care.
articles.evidence: Educational illustration; not a new guideline.

articles.title: Reading a clinical trial: relative versus absolute risk
articles.dek: A simple way to judge whether a statistically significant result will matter to patients.
summary: A treatment can sound dramatic when a study reports a relative risk reduction. But the absolute difference between groups often better communicates how much a typical patient may benefit.
For example, reducing an outcome from 2% to 1% is a 50% relative reduction but only a 1 percentage point absolute reduction. Study populations, harms and follow-up time still matter.
articles.why: Helps interpret new RCTs before translating them into clinical practice.

articles.title: What makes a new guideline practice-changing?
articles.dek: Look for patient-important outcomes, evidence certainty and implementation barriers.
summary: A new recommendation is not automatically a reason to change practice. First identify what changed from the previous version, the strength of evidence and whether the target population matches your patients.
Also consider whether a recommendation improves mortality, hospitalization or quality of life versus changing a surrogate marker alone.
articles.why: Provides a repeatable approach to assessing guideline updates.

articles.title: AI agents versus chatbots: what's the real difference?
articles.dek: From answering questions to coordinating tools and completing multi-step work.
summary: A chatbot primarily responds to prompts. An AI agent may also use tools, keep track of intermediate steps and act toward a defined goal, subject to permissions and oversight.

For a medical practice, potential applications include organizing administrative tasks or preparing summaries. Patient information requires careful attention to privacy, accuracy and approved systems.
articles.why: Understanding agents helps separate useful automation from marketing hype.
articles.evidence: Technology explainer; not a current product announcement.

articles.title: Why embodied AI is harder than text generation
articles.dek: Robots must understand uncertain physical environments, not just language.
summary: A language model can generate an instruction instantly, but a robot must perceive the world, plan movements and respond to unexpected changes. Errors have real physical consequences.
Progress depends on sensing, control, training data and robust safety systems working together.
articles.why: A useful lens for evaluating claims about humanoid robots.

articles.title: Building believable 3D towns with Godot and Blender
articles.dek: A practical pipeline for environments, characters and social simulation.
summary: Blender is used to create and animate 3D assets. Godot provides the game runtime, where characters move, interact and respond to game rules.
For a social-life simulator, start with one small playable neighborhood, a few characters and a repeatable daily routine before expanding the world.
articles.why: A practical foundation for an expandable social simulation game.
articles.evidence: Development explainer; not breaking gaming news.

articles.title: Can AI make non-player characters feel alive?
articles.dek: Memory, goals and constraints can make interactions feel more consistent.
summary: Traditional NPCs often follow scripted dialogue trees. AI-assisted systems can offer more flexible dialogue, but still need boundaries, memory design and predictable game mechanics.
The strongest approach may combine authored story structure with constrained dynamic conversations.
articles.why: Relevant to designing romance, careers and mysteries in simulation games.

articles.title: How a proposed policy becomes law in the United States
articles.dek: A neutral guide to bills, committees, votes and executive action.
summary: A proposal is not the same as an enacted law. Bills typically move through committee consideration and legislative votes, with differences between chambers resolved before a bill is presented to the president.
Executive actions, agency rules and court decisions follow different legal processes. When reading a headline, identifying the stage of the process can prevent misunderstandings.
articles.why: Helps distinguish announcements from actual legal changes.
articles.evidence: Civics explainer; not a report on a pending bill.

articles.title: A simple framework for reading geopolitical news
articles.dek: Separate verified events, competing claims and possible consequences.
summary: Geopolitical stories often mix confirmed events, statements by interested parties and predictions. A reliable briefing should label each separately and seek independent confirmation.
To understand why an event matters, examine its diplomatic, economic and humanitarian implications while acknowledging uncertainty and relevant competing perspectives.
articles.why: Makes complex world affairs easier to follow without oversimplifying.
